page: Vultr vhp-8c-16gb-intel is a High Performance family virtual server powered by an Intel Xeon x86_64 processor. The configuration features 8 vCPUs mapped to 4 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled, operating at a base clock speed of 2.0 GHz. It includes 16.0 GB of system memory, yielding a resource density of 2.0 GB per core. Local storage is bundled with 350 GB of NVMe SSD capacity, and the instance includes one complimentary public IPv4 address. The CPU allocation is shared, which introduces potential resource contention tradeoffs compared to dedicated instances.

Benchmark results place this server primarily in the average tier across standard compute and memory operations. The stress-ng single-core performance score of 1437.59 and multi-core score of 11603.93 align with mid-range expectations. Memory bandwidth tests show 831.82 GB/sec for cached small-block reads, dropping to 62.89 GB/sec for uncached large-block reads. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression is a notable bottleneck, scoring in the bottom 25% at 35.65 GB/sec. Similarly, while small 135M LLM inference runs at average speeds, scaling to a medium 7B model results in poor performance, with prompt processing dropping to 11.11 tokens/sec.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the shared CPU model and 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio provide a budget-friendly entry point for workloads requiring multi-core processing without sustained peak CPU utilization. It is well-suited for static web serving, where it achieves an average throughput of 8.38 GB/sec, and Redis database operations, which average 12.74 million operations per second. However, it is not recommended for heavy multi-threaded decompression tasks or medium-to-large LLM inference workloads due to performance degradation under sustained or complex computational loads.
description: Vultr vhp-8c-16gb-intel is an Intel Xeon-based virtual server from the High Performance family, configured with 8 shared vCPUs, 16.0 GB of RAM, and 350 GB of local NVMe SSD storage. Operating on the x86_64 architecture with 4 physical cores and hyper-threading, this server delivers average performance across most standard benchmarks, including a Passmark CPU score of 12523.23 and a Redis SET throughput of 12.74 million operations per second. However, its shared CPU allocation presents tradeoffs, as evidenced by weak multi-threaded bzip3 decompression and poor performance on medium 7B LLM inference tasks. This instance offers a cost-effective profile for workloads that do not require dedicated CPU resources, making it suitable for static web serving, basic database operations, and lightweight utility applications.
